newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. weather market leaves Europe feeds trade cold.
newsitem.headline: U.S. weather market leaves Europe feeds trade cold.

text.p: Unpredictable price swings on the CBOT soycomplex in the U.S. have undermined already depressed demand for meals and feeds in Europe, leaving traders handling only pockets of nearby business.
"We're living in a weather market and it has killed off business in Europe," Arie van Dijk, analyst at market statisticians Stigevo, said on Monday.
Traders said forecasts of hot, dry weather had been replaced by predictions of showers, taking the shine off prices in Project A trade and putting the market back on the defensive.
In the near term, Van Dijk said he expected a further cold front through the Midwest, bringing a 75 percent chance of rain to soy crop areas. Temperatures would also fall this week.
"It seems the weather will not be giving us any worries this week and crop conditions look good, for the moment," he said.
But traders said a degree of unpredictability remained.
"Chicago should open lower this afternoon, but you never know. It makes people very uncertain," said one senior trader.
As a result, no trades were reported in early Europe.
The strong dollar was another inhibiting factor, with traders saying that only a five to seven cent reduction in the mark rate would spark business.

Flood-related damage in central Europe was not a key market factor yet, but traders said they were keeping an eye on the situation. Poland was expected to have to import somewhere in the region of 450,000 tonnes of rapeseed due to crop losses.
Its rapeseed crop had already been cut by a severe winter and the recent floods had knocked another 100,000 tonnes off the expected harvest, traders said.
The harvest was now seen around 350,000 tonnes, against a crushing capacity of 800,000 tonnes, so imports were inevitable.
Van Dijk said he thought Germany, expecting a bumper rapeseed crop this year, would be the preferred market for Polish buyers as Canadian canola was still too expensive.
He reckoned the country would also need to import around 200,000 tonnes of rapemeal.
But in general the physical market was still plagued by slack demand.

Cattlefeed demand was seasonally depressed with cows grazing in fields, and pigfeed offtake in the Netherlands had been decimated by the swine fever epidemic. The two factors had combined to send some prices down to the bargain basement.
"Products such as citrus plup are historically low and in the next two months could fall even further," Van Dijk said.
The situation had been compounded by heavy arrivals into continental Europe from Brazil over the next quarter, he said.
"We could see prices recovering in the latter part of the year as consumers cover for the winter months, but not before."
